decisions.reason: The City's automated counter dataset can show whether it logged nearly 1.3 million bicycle passages by July 31, 2026.

The two readers split on this one. Traffic counts and corridor evaluations can show whether added cycling infrastructure shifted trips away from cars and reduced congestion. Against that: It is a general causal claim that a public record cannot definitively settle in either direction. It waits rather than being dropped.

The two readers split on this one. Before-and-after traffic counts can show whether converting traffic lanes caused slower travel, longer queues or more idling on affected corridors. Against that: It is a broad causal claim that a public record cannot definitively settle. It waits rather than being dropped.
Project plans and roadway records can show where traffic lanes were replaced by cycling infrastructure and whether this happened across the city.
Council minutes and the capital budget can show exactly what Council approved and whether the amount was $100 million.
The project's approved budget and scope can show whether $181 million covers roughly 600 metres of grade separation.
Edmonton's household travel survey can show what share of all trips, rather than only commutes, are made by bicycle.
The City's automated bike counter datasets record daily traffic volumes year-round. The two readers split GO and PARK.
The census and City transportation reports publish commute mode shares, so readers can learn whether bicycle commuting was below one percent.
The census reports commute modes for Edmonton and can show whether the car share was 87 percent.

The two readers split on this one. Monthly counter totals and commute data can show how much cycling persists through winter instead of treating cold-weather use as an all-or-nothing question. Against that: It is an opinion and not a factual proposition that a public record could settle. It waits rather than being dropped.
The City's winter bike counter datasets will show whether winter ridership has grown over the years. The two readers split GO and PARK.
The City's published snow-clearing priorities can show whether bike lanes are scheduled ahead of ordinary streets.
The operating budget and snow-and-ice service reports can show the annual amount assigned to maintaining cycling infrastructure.
Municipal budgets and public accounts can show how much road spending comes from property and general revenue rather than driver-specific charges.
The City's cycling-network map and open GIS data can classify the network and test the claimed 95 percent share.
City transportation planning processes and design standards document the approval requirements for routes. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Holyrood project plans and council records can show what the councillor proposed for the bike lane and school-bus loading area.
Project records, engagement reports, and council minutes will document why the design was stopped. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Official municipal election results report turnout directly and can settle whether it was below 40 percent.
Council's compensation and expense policy can show whether councillors receive a vehicle allowance and its amount.
Approved project plans can show which bike-lane installations removed parking and how many spaces were affected.
No public record can establish that nobody complained about the lane over an entire decade.

The two readers split on this one. The City's active transportation maps confirm the locations of bike lanes. Against that: The City map can settle the street name, but neither side's argument depends on whether the nearby lane is called 83 Avenue or Whyte Avenue. It waits rather than being dropped.
City road classification maps and project documents detail where lanes are built and road types. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Project timelines, source citations and engagement reports can show how old the underlying data was and which affected groups the City consulted.
This should reopen with a representative citywide survey and defined affected-neighbourhood results, since petitions and consultation responses cannot establish what most residents believe.
The capital budget can show whether the $100 million allocation covers one year or the full four-year cycle.
Capital-budget tables can test both the percentage calculation and what spending was classified as roads for cars.
Household Travel Surveys and bike counter data can verify usage percentages. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Census data and the Household Travel Survey report the percentage of the population that cycles. The two readers split GO and PARK.
The administration report and council agenda can show whether staff recommended pausing 14 routes for reassessment.
Council minutes and recorded votes can show whether the proposed pause and review failed.
Council motions and vote records can show who proposed the $50 million reduction, what the money would fund and whether Council rejected it.
The City's roadway-classification map can show whether the relevant stretch of 50 Street is officially a collector or an arterial.
Approved plans and the as-built cycling map can show whether 132 Avenue received bike lanes on both sides.
This should reopen when the staff positions responsible for the policy are identified and can be matched to published compensation records. The two readers split NO and PARK.
No public record can establish how many bicycles appeared in an observer's photograph during one hour at Heritage Days.
Procurement records and project reports can show which planned routes have completed design work or signed contracts and how much has been paid.
Government budgets and tax legislation can show where fuel taxes and registration revenue go and how much reaches Edmonton's roads.
Recorded council votes can show whether the same seven councillors repeatedly supported the bike-lane program.
Election results record votes, not what each voter knew or intended when casting a ballot.
Edmonton Fire Rescue Services and EMS response time reports or incident logs document delays caused by infrastructure. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Emergency-service policies and protected-lane design plans can show whether the lanes are built and authorized for emergency vehicles to use.
City accessibility and street-design standards can show whether protected lanes may incorporate wheelchair travel and accessible loading spaces.
This should reopen with representative observations or enforcement data comparing sidewalk and bike-lane use at defined locations. The two readers split NO and PARK.
City traffic diversion plans and road network maps will show if access from 119 Avenue to the alley was removed. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Provincial orders, bills and official notices can show whether Edmonton was directed to stop projects and whether legislation was scheduled.
City correspondence logs and council reports would confirm if written notice was received from the province. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Recall legislation and official petition notices can show both when a municipal recall is allowed and whether one has formally begun.
This should reopen with representative origin-to-destination travel-time data, since two personal commutes cannot establish the regional comparison.
No public record can settle whether the unreported encounters described by one rider occurred.
Successive City design standards and project files can show whether Edmonton progressed from painted lanes to barriers and full street reconstruction.
Budget shares and comparable travel-mode data can show whether cycling's funding is close to its measured use.
Capital budgets can show total road-building commitments and how much is assigned to the Yellowhead project.

The two readers split on this one. Capital budget documents will provide the cost of the 50 Street project to compare against the active transportation budget. Against that: Once the two approved amounts are established, whether $181 million is nearly double $100 million is settled arithmetic. It waits rather than being dropped.
Residents paying general taxes while also riding bicycles is an ordinary feature of the tax system that neither side meaningfully disputes.
Census profile data cross-referenced by commuting mode reports demographics by transportation choice. The two readers split GO and PARK.
A household travel survey can show whether most residents who cycle also drive or live in vehicle-owning households.
Municipal taxes funding shared services regardless of each resident's personal use is an undisputed feature of public finance.

The two readers split on this one. Parking inventories, fee schedules and street costs can show what taxpayers provide when curb parking is offered without a user charge. Against that: This is an abstract economic proposition rather than a specific factual claim a local public record can settle. It waits rather than being dropped.
The cycling-network map and official road classifications can show whether any bike lanes occupy arterial roads.
Project reports can show whether lane reductions were approved as traffic calming and bike lanes were added during the same work.
The hearing's speaker list and submissions can show how many participants supported and opposed the lanes.
No public record identifies who was paid to attend the meeting, so the allegation cannot be settled in either direction.
City accessibility audits and DATS operational reports would document access issues caused by barriers. The two readers split GO and PARK.
This should reopen when local travel-access and health data can compare residents before and after the network changes. The two readers split NO and PARK.

The two readers split on this one. As-built plans can show whether the lanes physically separate riders, including children and families, from motor traffic. Against that: This is a definitional truism of a protected bike lane. It waits rather than being dropped.
The network map can show whether a continuous protected or low-traffic route connects 104 Street and 124 Street, the concrete part of the safety claim.
Provincial traffic law and City bylaws can show where cyclists may legally ride when no bike lane is present.
Census tables linking occupation and commute mode can show whether Edmonton residents in blue-collar occupations cycle to work.
Police collision records can show what share of reported bicycle crashes assigned a contributing action to the cyclist, which is narrower and clearer than personal blame.
Network maps and project plans can show whether new routes connect to destinations and existing cycling infrastructure or end in gaps.
Cycling and LRT maps can identify breaks in routes serving stations and following the rail corridor.
Project design documents and road cross-sections specify whether the road width is increased. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City road design guidelines and project cross-sections detail the lane widths provided for passing. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City pavement condition index reports and maintenance logs will show wear patterns in remaining lanes. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City snow clearing policies and operational guidelines document where windrows are to be placed. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City traffic volume studies and school zone traffic assessments will show the function of 79 Street. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Archived ETS maps and service-change reports can show whether the relevant community bus routes were removed.
Traffic-control plans and posted-speed records can show whether streets such as 92 Street operate as single-file 30 km/h shared roads.
Council reports and budget options can show whether administration presented two snow-removal proposals and whether both required more spending.
Council agendas and administration reports can show whether a calcium-chloride proposal was scheduled for debate.
The meeting video, chair's ruling and speaker queue can show whether speaking time fell from five minutes to three and whether 70 speakers remained.
Procurement deadlines and project schedules can show whether the routes could still be tendered for the 2026 construction season.
City urban canopy reports and zoning impact assessments document tree loss and parking changes from infill. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Census and City planning data can show how quickly Edmonton grew and whether single-family homes still predominate, the factual basis of the sprawl argument.
Efficient is undefined here, so no record could settle the claim without choosing a measure such as capacity, cost, time or emissions.
That roads carry deliveries, buses and emergency vehicles is a truism accepted by both sides of this argument.
Household travel surveys can compare bicycle trips by purpose and distance to show whether recreation outweighs commuting.
City snow clearing operational reports and road width measurements during winter document this. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City parking management records and project traffic accommodation plans will show parking restrictions on that street. The two readers split GO and PARK.
The project limits and official school locations can show how many schools sit on the affected stretch of 132 Avenue.
Council records and signed City agreements can show whether Edmonton formally committed to becoming a 15-minute city.
Edmonton's zoning bylaw can show whether developments remain subject to minimum parking requirements.
LRT schedules and annual collision reports can test both average travel speed and whether deaths have increased year by year.
Barely functions has no defined measure, so ridership and reliability records could not produce a verdict on this wording.
The capital budget and infrastructure-deficit reports can show whether both amounts were presented at the same time and what each covers.
This should reopen after the claim is narrowed to defined services, measures and dates that pavement ratings and service reports can answer.
EPCOR drainage reports and insurance claims data presented to council document damage costs. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Capital project budgets and utility cost reports will show the financial impact of new streetlights. The two readers split GO and PARK.

The two readers split on this one. The City's property tax assessment rolls and tax rate history can confirm these specific increases for typical properties. Against that: Property-tax rates cannot verify the private tax bills or assessment changes described by two individual residents. It waits rather than being dropped.
Capital budgets and council amendments can show whether funding left the west-end recreation-centre project and was redirected to active transportation.
This alleges a private conflict involving an identifiable person, and the site has no right-of-reply process for such accusations.
Project and procurement records can show when the 189 Street lane was installed, when it was removed and what each step cost.
Council and project records can show what role the former councillor had in approving or championing the 189 Street lane.
Municipal council and project records can show whether Canadian cities have formally removed bike lanes and whether the examples amount to a broader trend.
Business license cancellation records exist, but proving they closed specifically due to access issues requires studies that may not exist. The two readers split NO and PARK.
City plans, bylaws and council motions can show whether a year-round downtown car ban is actually proposed.
Street Lab evaluations, speed measurements and collision data can show how the projects changed traffic and pedestrian safety.
Before-and-after collision and injury data can show whether protected routes changed cycling risk on Edmonton streets.
No public record comprehensively tracks how each office-holder travels to work, so the claim cannot be settled in either direction.
